B) No. The opposition remains divided, coordinates poorly, or suffers defections and tactical failures, allowing the leading bloc to win many districts with pluralities.

Will Hungary’s mixed electoral system and seat-allocation rules convert the leading bloc’s vote share into a disproportionately large parliamentary majority in 2026?
A) Yes. The electoral system’s mechanics strongly amplify the leading bloc’s advantage, so a vote margin that might look insufficient in proportional terms still yields a realistic path to two-thirds of seats.
B) No. The electoral system does not amplify the winner as much as expected in this cycle, or conversely it amplifies the winner even more than skeptics expected because district results are lopsided and compensation mechanics favor the leader.

Will there be major pre-election economic deterioration or a salient governance scandal that meaningfully weakens the incumbent bloc?
A) Yes. Economic pain, corruption revelations, or visible governing failures significantly erode incumbent support before election day.
B) No. The economy stabilizes, scandals fail to bite, or voter perceptions do not translate these issues into large electoral losses for the incumbent.

Will any new or revived challenger on the right or center-right split votes that would otherwise go to Fidesz-KDNP in key districts or on the party list?
A) Yes. A credible competitor draws away enough incumbent-leaning voters to reduce district wins and seat efficiency for Fidesz-KDNP.
B) No. Potential challengers fail to emerge, remain marginal, or collapse, leaving the incumbent side’s vote consolidated.

Will turnout and mobilization patterns disproportionately favor the side best positioned to win single-member constituencies by large margins?
A) Yes. Differential turnout favors the opposition or otherwise compresses the incumbent’s district advantage, making a seat landslide less likely.
B) No. Turnout patterns favor the incumbent’s stronger machine and rural base, magnifying district wins and seat disproportionality.

Will there be meaningful changes in electoral law, coalition structure, candidate eligibility, or administrative conditions before the election that materially affect the odds of a supermajority?
A) Yes. Institutional or legal changes occur that reduce the leading bloc’s seat-conversion advantage or otherwise make a supermajority harder to achieve.
B) No. Rules and administrative conditions remain favorable to the status quo, or changes unexpectedly further benefit the dominant bloc and increase supermajority chances.

Will the opposition’s organizational capacity and candidate quality in local districts be strong enough to convert anti-incumbent sentiment into constituency wins?
A) Yes. The opposition fields stronger local candidates, runs more disciplined campaigns, and performs much better in constituency contests than expected.
B) No. Opposition organizations remain weak, local candidates underperform, and anti-incumbent votes do not translate efficiently into constituency victories.

Will external shocks or geopolitical developments shortly before the election increase rally-around-incumbent effects rather than anti-incumbent backlash?
A) Yes. A late external event benefits the opposition or harms the government, reducing the incumbent’s chances of a sweeping mandate.
B) No. A geopolitical or security shock produces a rally-around-incumbent effect and boosts support for the governing bloc.

Will polling and public indicators before the election accurately capture true voter preferences and district-level competitiveness?
A) Yes. Pre-election polling and public data are broadly reliable and correctly show a race too competitive for a supermajority.
B) No. Polling and public indicators systematically understate the leading bloc’s support or misread district-level races, causing forecasters to miss a path to a supermajority.

Will the electoral environment in 2026 convert a merely clear plurality for the leading bloc into a realistic path to two-thirds of seats?
A) The electoral system and district structure will strongly magnify a solid lead into a plausible two-thirds seat outcome.
B) The electoral system and district structure will not convert an ordinary lead into a plausible two-thirds seat outcome without an exceptionally large vote margin.

Will Fidesz-KDNP enter the 2026 election with national support strong enough to dominate most single-member districts?
A) Fidesz-KDNP will retain support high enough to win an overwhelming share of single-member districts.
B) Fidesz-KDNP will not have support strong enough to dominate enough single-member districts for a supermajority.

Will the anti-Fidesz opposition coordinate effectively enough in constituencies to prevent seat amplification for the leading bloc?
A) Opposition forces will remain fragmented or ineffective at constituency coordination, allowing the leading bloc to sweep many districts.
B) Opposition forces will coordinate effectively enough in constituencies to block a district sweep by the leading bloc.

Will there be election-rule, districting, or administrative conditions before 2026 that materially advantage the incumbent bloc beyond current baseline expectations?
A) Pre-election institutional or administrative conditions will materially increase the incumbent bloc’s seat-conversion advantage.
B) Pre-election institutional or administrative conditions will not materially expand the incumbent bloc’s advantage beyond the usual baseline.

Will any coalition capable of winning a supermajority remain sufficiently unified before and after the election to count as a single governing bloc for this question?
A) A supermajority-capable alliance will function as a coherent single bloc for purposes of winning and holding a supermajority.
B) No alliance capable of reaching a supermajority will be coherent enough to count as a single bloc able to win and sustain it.

Will one electoral bloc enter the 2026 election with a large enough national vote advantage over all rivals to plausibly convert that lead into two-thirds of seats?
A) No. The leading bloc’s vote margin will be too modest for a two-thirds seat outcome.
B) Yes. One bloc will hold a sufficiently large vote lead that two-thirds of seats is realistically within reach.

Will the anti-incumbent opposition coordinate effectively in single-member districts rather than fragmenting the vote?
A) Yes. The opposition will coordinate well enough in constituencies to prevent the leading bloc from piling up district wins.
B) No. The opposition will remain fragmented or poorly coordinated, allowing the leading bloc to win many districts with pluralities.

Will the electoral system’s seat-conversion mechanics in 2026 strongly magnify the leading bloc’s seat share relative to its vote share?
A) No. The system will not amplify the winner enough to turn an ordinary victory into a supermajority.
B) Yes. The system will heavily magnify the winner, making a supermajority possible from a much smaller vote margin.

Will the governing camp retain enough support in marginal and competitive constituencies to sweep a very large share of single-member districts?
A) No. The governing camp will lose enough swing constituencies that a supermajority path becomes narrow.
B) Yes. The governing camp will hold most competitive constituencies and rack up an overwhelming district tally.

Will there be major pre-election legal, districting, or administrative changes that further increase the leading bloc’s ability to reach a two-thirds seat share?
A) No. There will be no significant new institutional changes that further tilt seat conversion toward a supermajority.
B) Yes. Institutional, legal, districting, or administrative changes will further improve the leading bloc’s supermajority chances.

Will turnout and voter mobilization patterns disproportionately favor the bloc already best positioned to win many constituencies?
A) No. Turnout/mobilization will not systematically advantage the bloc best placed for a seat landslide.
B) Yes. Differential turnout/mobilization will especially benefit the bloc already advantaged in constituency races.

Will any new or minor parties siphon enough votes from the main challenger(s) to make a supermajority for the leading bloc more attainable?
A) No. Minor parties will not meaningfully split the anti-incumbent vote in ways that help produce a supermajority.
B) Yes. Minor or new parties will split challenger votes enough to ease the leading bloc’s path to two-thirds.

Will the election environment be broadly free and competitive enough that national vote swings translate into corresponding seat gains for challengers?
A) Yes. The electoral environment will be competitive enough that challengers can convert support into seat gains, reducing supermajority odds.
B) No. Structural constraints on competitiveness will blunt challengers’ ability to translate votes into seats, raising supermajority odds.

Will Fidesz and its allies enter the 2026 election with enough unified organizational and political coherence to function as a single seat-maximizing bloc nationwide?
A) Yes. Forecasters on this side expect the incumbent camp to remain disciplined, allied partners to stay aligned, and candidate placement plus list strategy to be optimized for maximizing seats.
B) Yes, but in the opposite sense: forecasters on this side expect the incumbent bloc to remain cohesive while opponents remain fractured, giving the largest bloc a decisive organizational edge in district contests.

Will the main opposition forces coordinate effectively enough in single-member districts to prevent widespread anti-incumbent vote splitting?
A) Yes. Forecasters on this side expect opposition parties to avoid major coordination failures, withdraw weaker candidates where needed, and focus on defeating the incumbent in districts rather than preserving separate brands.
B) No. Forecasters on this side expect opposition coordination to be partial, unstable, or undermined by ideological incompatibilities, personal rivalries, and local-level candidate conflicts.

Will the electoral system and district map continue to produce a strong seat bonus for the largest bloc in 2026, relative to its national vote share?
A) No. Forecasters on this side think the seat bonus will be limited by improved opposition coordination, competitive districts, and the practical ceiling on disproportionality.
B) Yes. Forecasters on this side think Hungary’s rules and district structure still grant a large conversion bonus to the leading bloc, so a modest vote lead can become an outsized seat share.

Will Fidesz lead the national party-list vote by a margin large enough that district-level advantages could plausibly convert it into a two-thirds parliamentary majority?
A) No. Forecasters on this side think even if Fidesz remains first, its vote-share lead will likely be too small for a two-thirds outcome once the opposition consolidates.
B) Yes. Forecasters on this side think Fidesz could win by a sufficiently clear national margin that, combined with electoral mechanics, a two-thirds majority becomes realistic.

Will late campaign dynamics or pre-election rule changes materially improve the incumbent bloc’s chances of turning a normal majority into a supermajority?
A) No. Forecasters on this side expect rules and campaign conditions to stay broadly within already-known parameters, with no major extra boost to supermajority odds.
B) Yes. Forecasters on this side think legal, administrative, media, or campaign-environment shifts before the election could further tilt the playing field toward a supermajority outcome.

Will turnout and voter mobilization patterns disproportionately benefit the bloc best positioned to sweep competitive single-member districts?
A) No. Forecasters on this side expect mobilization to be high enough across the opposition electorate that the incumbent cannot dominate marginal districts purely through turnout asymmetry.
B) Yes. Forecasters on this side expect turnout and GOTV asymmetries to favor the incumbent enough to flip many close districts, especially if opposition enthusiasm or discipline weakens.

Will any post-election alliance, defection, or support arrangement realistically allow a largest bloc that falls short on election night to reach a durable two-thirds governing majority?
A) No. Forecasters on this side think two-thirds support would need to be won electorally; post-election bargaining or defections are too unreliable or politically costly to matter. 
B) Yes. Forecasters on this side think a bloc that falls somewhat short on election night could still secure two-thirds support through allied micro-parties, independents, or defections on key constitutional votes.

Will the leading anti-Fidesz forces remain sufficiently fragmented in single-member districts that Fidesz can win many seats with only pluralities rather than outright majorities?
A) Yes. Opposition parties and challengers will remain divided, allowing the leading bloc to sweep many constituencies through vote-splitting.
B) No. Anti-Fidesz voting will be more effectively coordinated, reducing wasted opposition votes in single-member districts.

Will Fidesz retain a large enough nationwide vote share by 2026 that the electoral system can plausibly convert it into two-thirds of seats?
A) Yes. Fidesz will remain strong enough nationally that, once amplified by the system, a supermajority remains within reach.
B) No. Fidesz’s national vote share will be too low for even a favorable system to deliver two-thirds of seats.

Do Hungary’s electoral rules, district map, and incumbency/media advantages still provide a large seat bonus to the leading bloc in 2026?
A) Yes. Structural advantages remain powerful and continue to over-reward the largest bloc in seats relative to votes.
B) No. The remaining institutional advantages are insufficient by themselves to create another constitutional majority under current political conditions.

Will any opposition alliance or alternative governing coalition be organizationally coherent enough to avoid self-defeating coordination failures before the election?
A) No. Opposition actors will not coordinate effectively enough to prevent avoidable losses in key districts.
B) Yes. Opposition parties or other anti-incumbent forces will coordinate well enough to contest districts competitively.

Will economic conditions, corruption scandals, or broader anti-incumbent sentiment materially erode support for the ruling bloc before 2026?
A) No. Incumbent erosion will be limited; economic and scandal effects will not significantly dent ruling-party dominance.
B) Yes. Economic malaise, scandals, or anti-incumbent sentiment will substantially weaken the ruling bloc before the election.

If no single party reaches two-thirds on its own, is there a realistic path for a post-election coalition to hold a disciplined supermajority?
A) Yes. If needed, a compatible ally or coalition arrangement could supply the extra seats and maintain discipline.
B) No. Post-election coalition arithmetic and ideological incompatibilities make a disciplined supermajority coalition unrealistic.

Will the leading anti-Fidesz opposition forces coordinate effectively enough in single-member districts to avoid major anti-incumbent vote-splitting in 2026?
A) Yes. The main opposition forces will cooperate or strategically stand down in enough constituencies that anti-Fidesz votes are not heavily fragmented.
B) No. The opposition will remain meaningfully fragmented, with coordination failures or rival candidacies in enough constituencies to prevent efficient seat conversion by the anti-Fidesz side.

Will Fidesz-KDNP enter the election with a sufficiently large nationwide vote advantage over its nearest effective rival or rival bloc to make a supermajority seat bonus plausible?
A) Yes. Fidesz-KDNP will hold a clear enough national lead that, combined with incumbency advantages, a supermajority becomes realistically attainable.
B) No. Fidesz-KDNP will not maintain a sufficiently large national lead; the race will be close enough, or the incumbent advantage narrow enough, that a supermajority becomes unlikely.

Will the electoral system and district-level map convert the likely vote distribution into a seat share large enough for some bloc to reach the supermajority threshold?
A) Yes. Given the likely geography of support and electoral rules, the winning bloc’s vote share will be translated into an exceptionally large seat share, potentially crossing the supermajority line.
B) No. Even if one bloc wins clearly, the vote-to-seat conversion will not be extreme enough in 2026 to produce the required supermajority.

Will there be a major late-breaking political realignment, coalition restructuring, or opposition collapse before the election that substantially concentrates seats in favor of one bloc?
A) Yes. A significant realignment or collapse will occur that sharply concentrates parliamentary seats in one bloc’s favor.
B) No. There will be no major realignment or collapse; competition will remain structured such that seats are not unusually concentrated in one bloc.

How unified and electorally effective will the main anti-incumbent opposition be by the time of the election?
A) The opposition will remain fragmented, fail to coordinate effectively in many constituencies, and underperform nationally.
B) The opposition will consolidate behind a viable challenger or coordination mechanism and avoid large vote-splitting losses.

How large will the leading party or coalition’s national vote advantage be over its nearest rival?
A) The leading party or coalition will win a clear national lead large enough to make a supermajority arithmetically plausible.
B) The national vote will be relatively close, making a two-thirds seat outcome very difficult even for the winner.

Will the single-member district results break strongly enough toward one side to create a large seat bonus beyond proportional vote share?
A) Single-member districts will tilt heavily toward the leading side, producing many narrow wins and a large seat bonus.
B) District contests will be competitive enough that the winner gains only a modest seat bonus over its vote share.

Will the electoral rules, district boundaries, and election administration remain materially favorable to the incumbent side through 2026?
A) The institutional environment will continue to favor the incumbent side in ways that materially increase the odds of crossing the two-thirds seat threshold.
B) The rules and administration will not provide enough additional structural advantage to push the leading side to a supermajority.

Will there be a significant late shift in public sentiment caused by economic conditions or a major political scandal before the election?
A) Economic and political conditions will stay stable enough, or move in the incumbent’s favor enough, to preserve strong support through election day.
B) Economic deterioration or a major scandal will significantly weaken the incumbent before the election and reduce the chance of a supermajority.

Will the electoral rules, district map, and electoral administration in force for 2026 remain at least as favorable to Fidesz/the incumbent bloc as in prior elections?
A) Yes. The institutional setup in 2026 will remain broadly as favorable to the incumbent bloc as in prior cycles.
B) No. Institutional or administrative conditions in 2026 will be less favorable to the incumbent bloc than in prior cycles.

Will the opposition enter the 2026 election in a fragmented way across many single-member districts rather than with disciplined coordination or a unified front?
A) Yes. Opposition parties will mostly remain fragmented or poorly coordinated in districts, splitting anti-Fidesz votes.
B) No. The opposition will achieve meaningful coordination or unification in districts, reducing vote splitting.

Will Fidesz-KDNP retain a national vote share and district-level competitiveness close to its recent election performance by the time of the 2026 election?
A) Yes. Fidesz-KDNP will remain electorally strong enough nationally and locally to contend for another oversized seat share.
B) No. Fidesz-KDNP’s vote share and district-level strength will decline materially relative to recent elections.

Will major anti-incumbent shocks before the election (for example severe economic deterioration, scandal, or elite defection) be limited enough that they do not materially erode the governing bloc’s seat conversion?
A) Yes. No sufficiently large anti-incumbent shock will occur to substantially undermine the governing bloc before voting day.
B) No. A major adverse shock will occur and significantly weaken the governing bloc’s electoral position.

Will any opposition coalition or challenger bloc become organizationally coherent and popular enough to win a large number of single-member districts against Fidesz?
A) No. No opposition formation will become strong and coherent enough to take many districts from Fidesz.
B) Yes. An opposition coalition or challenger bloc will become sufficiently coherent and competitive to win many districts.

Will turnout and voter mobilization patterns in 2026 resemble recent cycles in ways that favor the incumbent bloc’s seat efficiency rather than produce an opposition-skewed surge?
A) Yes. Mobilization patterns will remain broadly consistent with recent elections and will not generate a large opposition seat bonus.
B) No. Turnout and mobilization will shift in a way that disproportionately benefits the opposition and reduces the incumbent bloc’s seat efficiency.

Will the anti-Fidesz opposition be sufficiently unified in candidate coordination and alliance structure to avoid major vote-splitting in single-member districts in 2026?
A) The opposition will remain meaningfully fragmented or only loosely coordinated, causing significant vote-splitting in many single-member districts.
B) The opposition will achieve effective coordination or unity, minimizing vote-splitting in single-member districts.

Will Fidesz-KDNP (or another leading bloc) retain a national vote share high enough to make a two-thirds seat outcome realistically attainable under Hungary’s electoral system?
A) The leading incumbent bloc will still command a strong enough national vote share that, combined with district wins, a supermajority is within reach.
B) The leading incumbent bloc’s national vote share will fall too low for a supermajority to be realistically achievable, even if it remains the largest force.

Will Hungary’s electoral system and district-level geography in 2026 produce a large seat bonus for the leading bloc relative to its national vote share?
A) The electoral system and constituency map will continue to translate a modest lead in votes into a disproportionately large lead in seats for the top bloc.
B) The vote-to-seat conversion in 2026 will be less distortive, so even a clear lead in votes will not yield a two-thirds seat share.

Will minor parties outside the main opposition bloc win enough votes or district-level influence to materially split the anti-incumbent electorate?
A) Smaller parties or breakaway actors will siphon enough opposition-oriented votes to weaken anti-incumbent coordination in many races.
B) Smaller parties will not materially fragment the anti-incumbent vote, either because they remain weak or because coordination contains their impact.

Will pre-election political and economic conditions by 2026 substantially erode incumbent support relative to previous parliamentary elections?
A) Conditions will not deteriorate enough to cause a major collapse in incumbent support; the ruling bloc will remain broadly resilient.
B) Political and economic conditions will significantly weaken the incumbents, reducing their electoral strength compared with prior cycles.

Will the leading bloc in 2026 be able to convert a modest national popular-vote lead into a disproportionately large seat bonus under Hungary’s mixed electoral system?
A) Yes. The electoral system is likely to magnify the leading bloc’s advantage enough that a modest vote lead can still yield a two-thirds seat outcome.
B) No. The seat bonus is unlikely to be large enough to turn only a modest vote lead into a supermajority; two-thirds would require a much stronger underlying electoral performance.

Will anti-incumbent parties coordinate candidate entry and vote transfers effectively enough in single-member districts to prevent the dominant bloc from sweeping a large majority of constituencies?
A) No. Opposition coordination is likely to remain incomplete or uneven, allowing the dominant bloc to win many constituencies with pluralities.
B) Yes. Anti-incumbent coordination is likely to improve enough that many constituencies become one-on-one contests, sharply reducing seat overconversion.

By 2026, will the incumbent camp retain enough geographic strength in rural and small-town districts to win most marginal constituencies even if the national race is relatively close?
A) Yes. The incumbent camp is likely to preserve a durable territorial advantage outside major urban centers, which will be decisive in district contests.
B) No. The incumbent camp’s geographic edge is likely to erode enough that many rural and small-town marginals become genuinely competitive.

Is it likely that any post-election alliance capable of crossing the supermajority threshold would be sufficiently cohesive and formalized to count as a genuine governing coalition rather than an unstable arithmetic possibility?
A) Yes. If the numbers exist, the alliance is likely to be formal and disciplined enough to function as a real supermajority coalition.
B) No. Even if seat arithmetic briefly permits it, a cross-threshold alliance is unlikely to be cohesive and formal enough to count as a stable supermajority coalition.

Will the opposition enter 2026 with sufficiently effective coordination or coalition discipline in single-member districts to prevent major anti-incumbent vote fragmentation?
A) Yes. Opposition actors will coordinate candidacies and tactical voting well enough in many constituencies that anti-Fidesz votes are not badly split.
B) No. Opposition fragmentation, local rivalries, or failed alliance management will leave many districts with split anti-Fidesz voting.

Will Fidesz retain enough nationwide support and district-level strength by 2026 to finish clearly first in most single-member constituencies?
A) No. Fidesz will suffer enough erosion that it will not dominate most constituencies, making a supermajority much harder.
B) Yes. Fidesz will remain the dominant national force and the strongest contender in a large majority of constituencies.

Will Hungary’s electoral rules, districting, and campaign environment in 2026 continue to grant a large seat-conversion advantage to the leading bloc, potentially enough to turn a plurality into a supermajority?
A) No. The system still favors the largest bloc, but not enough by itself to reliably generate a supermajority without very strong underlying vote dominance.
B) Yes. The electoral and campaign environment can still magnify a modest lead into a disproportionately large seat majority, possibly even a supermajority.

Will there be significant rule changes, administrative interventions, or opposition constraints before the election that materially increase the likelihood that the incumbent bloc converts votes into a two-thirds majority?
A) No. Pre-election interventions will be limited or marginal, so baseline political competition rather than institutional engineering will determine the seat outcome.
B) Yes. Additional rule changes or administrative asymmetries will materially tilt the playing field further toward an incumbent supermajority outcome.

Will anti-incumbent pressures by 2026—especially economic strain, scandal, elite splits, or mobilized tactical voting—be strong enough to overcome incumbency advantages and sharply reduce Fidesz’s seat share?
A) Yes. Voter dissatisfaction and strategic anti-incumbent behavior will be strong enough to break the incumbency machine in many districts.
B) No. Anti-incumbent pressures will remain too weak or too diffuse to offset incumbency, media dominance, and organizational advantages.

Will the leading incumbent bloc (most plausibly Fidesz-KDNP) enter the 2026 election with national support high enough that, under Hungary’s electoral system, a two-thirds parliamentary majority is realistically within reach?
A) Yes. The incumbent bloc’s support is sufficiently high, stable, and geographically efficient that a two-thirds seat outcome is genuinely attainable.
B) No. The incumbent bloc’s support falls below the level needed for a plausible two-thirds seat conversion, even with institutional advantages.

Will anti-incumbent opposition parties coordinate effectively enough in single-member districts to prevent the leading party from converting a plurality into a landslide seat bonus?
A) Yes. Opposition coordination succeeds in many districts, sharply reducing the incumbent’s seat bonus and making a supermajority unlikely.
B) No. Opposition coordination fails or only partially works, leaving many districts split and allowing the leading party to rack up constituency wins.

Will the structure and administration of the electoral system in 2026 remain at least as favorable to the leading incumbent party as in prior elections?
A) Yes. District boundaries, compensation rules, media environment, and election administration continue to favor the incumbent enough to boost seat conversion.
B) No. The electoral framework is less favorable than expected to the incumbent, whether through legal changes, administration, monitoring, or reduced asymmetry.

Will there be major fragmentation, defection, or organizational weakening within the dominant incumbent camp before the election?
A) Yes. The incumbent camp experiences meaningful elite splits, defections, or local organizational decay that reduce its ability to dominate districts.
B) No. The incumbent camp remains disciplined, cohesive, and organizationally strong through election day.

Will the opposition side remain too fragmented, unpopular, or strategically incoherent to present a credible nationwide alternative?
A) No. The opposition remains divided or ineffective, allowing the leading party to dominate constituency races and overperform in seats.
B) Yes. The opposition becomes more unified, credible, and strategically disciplined, limiting district losses and reducing supermajority chances.

Will economic and social conditions by the election be good enough, or perceived as good enough, to preserve broad incumbent support?
A) Yes. Inflation, growth, public services, and general mood are good enough—or blamed insufficiently on the government—that incumbent support holds up.
B) No. Economic pain, corruption fatigue, or policy backlash seriously weakens the incumbent’s support by election time.

Will there be a late campaign shock or external event that materially shifts vote intention or turnout in a way that affects supermajority odds?
A) Yes. A scandal, crisis, war-related shock, corruption revelation, leadership event, or mobilization surprise meaningfully changes the race late.
B) No. No major late shock occurs, or shocks that do occur are quickly absorbed and do not significantly alter the seat trajectory.

Will turnout composition favor the leading incumbent party strongly enough that its vote converts unusually efficiently into seats?
A) Yes. Differential turnout benefits the incumbent because its voters are more disciplined and better distributed across winnable districts.
B) No. Turnout composition is neutral or opposition-favoring, reducing the incumbent’s ability to translate support into extra seats.

Will smaller parties near the threshold mostly fail to enter parliament, thereby amplifying the largest bloc’s seat share?
A) Yes. Enough minor-party votes are wasted below threshold that the largest bloc receives a substantial seat premium.
B) No. Most relevant smaller parties clear thresholds, so fewer votes are wasted and the largest bloc gains less seat amplification.

Will any post-election coalition arrangement capable of producing a supermajority be politically feasible, even if no single list wins one outright?
A) Yes. A workable alliance after the vote could combine parties into a two-thirds majority even without a single-list sweep.
B) No. No politically feasible post-election coalition exists that would create a supermajority; seat totals must be won more directly.

Will the anti-Fidesz opposition be sufficiently unified in candidacies and list strategy to avoid major vote-splitting in most competitive districts by the 2026 election?
A) The anti-Fidesz opposition will remain insufficiently unified, with meaningful fragmentation or coordination failures across many districts.
B) The anti-Fidesz opposition will be sufficiently unified to prevent major vote-splitting across most competitive districts.

Will Fidesz enter the 2026 election with national voter support strong enough to finish far ahead of any rival bloc?
A) Fidesz will retain sufficiently strong national support to finish decisively ahead of any rival bloc.
B) Fidesz will not retain enough national support to finish far ahead of rivals.

Will the electoral system and district-level seat conversion still amplify the largest party or coalition enough that a clear lead in votes can translate into a two-thirds parliamentary supermajority?
A) The electoral system and district-level dynamics will still strongly magnify the leading party’s seat share, making a supermajority conversion plausible.
B) The electoral system and district-level dynamics will not magnify the leading party enough to make a supermajority likely.

Will the political and economic environment before the election favor incumbents rather than generate a strong anti-government swing?
A) The pre-election political and economic environment will be relatively favorable to the incumbent government, limiting anti-government swing.
B) The pre-election political and economic environment will generate a substantial anti-government swing against the incumbent government.

Will the leading bloc in 2026 win enough single-member districts for the electoral system to generate a seat bonus large enough to make a two-thirds majority realistic?
A) Yes. The leading bloc will dominate enough single-member districts that the mixed system can plausibly translate its support into a supermajority of seats.
B) No. The leading bloc will not win enough single-member districts for a two-thirds seat bonus to be realistic.

Will the anti-Fidesz opposition remain sufficiently fragmented in district-level competition that the leading governing bloc can win many seats with pluralities rather than majorities?
A) Yes. Opposition fragmentation will persist, allowing the leading governing bloc to capture many districts with divided opposition votes.
B) No. The opposition will coordinate effectively enough that district races are mostly consolidated rather than fragmented.

Will Fidesz-KDNP retain a clear national vote advantage by 2026 rather than face a close race or opposition lead?
A) Yes. Fidesz-KDNP will maintain a meaningful nationwide vote lead by 2026.
B) No. Fidesz-KDNP will face a close contest, significant erosion, or even trail nationally by 2026.

Will there be any electoral-law, district-boundary, or seat-allocation changes before the election that materially increase the leading incumbent bloc’s chances of converting votes into a two-thirds seat share?
A) Yes. Any legal or administrative changes before 2026 will, on net, make it easier for the incumbent bloc to secure a disproportionate seat share.
B) No. There will be no meaningful rules changes favoring seat conversion, or changes will not materially affect supermajority odds.

If no single party wins two-thirds alone, is a post-election coalition or alliance likely to form that would control at least two-thirds of parliamentary seats?
A) Yes. Even absent a solo supermajority, allied parties would likely cooperate after the election and jointly exceed the two-thirds threshold.
B) No. A two-thirds post-election coalition is unlikely because seat totals will be too fragmented or potential partners will not align.

Will turnout and voter mobilization patterns in 2026 favor the incumbent bloc’s ability to overperform in constituencies relative to national polling?
A) Yes. Turnout composition and campaign mobilization will favor the incumbent bloc in decisive districts, boosting seat conversion.
B) No. Turnout and mobilization will not systematically advantage the incumbent bloc in constituency outcomes.

Will new parties or splinter movements on the opposition side draw enough votes to prevent effective anti-incumbent coordination in key districts?
A) Yes. New or splinter opposition forces will siphon enough support to undermine one-on-one district contests against incumbents.
B) No. New or splinter parties will not materially disrupt anti-incumbent coordination in the districts that matter most.

Will Fidesz-KDNP enter the 2026 election as a unified, electorally dominant bloc with no meaningful elite split on the right?
A) Yes. The ruling alliance will remain cohesive, with no major defection or viable challenger on the right, preserving a single dominant vehicle for a supermajority.
B) No. The ruling camp will face meaningful internal strain, defections, or a credible right-wing alternative that dilutes the only plausible supermajority vehicle.

Will the opposition coordinate effectively enough in single-member districts to prevent large-scale vote splitting against the leading incumbent candidate?
A) Yes. Opposition parties or candidates will coordinate unusually well, limiting three-way and four-way splits and reducing the incumbent’s seat bonus.
B) No. The opposition will fail to coordinate consistently, but not to the extent needed for the incumbent to rack up enough district wins for two-thirds; or coordination will be good enough in key districts to block a supermajority.

Will the national vote margin between Fidesz-KDNP and its nearest coordinated rival be large enough for Hungary’s electoral system to translate it into a two-thirds seat bonus?
A) Yes. Even a moderate popular-vote lead for Fidesz-KDNP will likely be efficiently distributed, and the electoral system can magnify that lead into a supermajority.
B) No. The incumbent’s vote lead will be too small, too unevenly distributed, or too diluted for electoral mechanics alone to generate a two-thirds seat share.

Will economic conditions and household perceptions by election time be good enough to avoid a substantial anti-incumbent swing?

Will turnout and voter mobilization patterns disproportionately benefit the largest existing governing bloc rather than a unified challenger coalition?
A) Turnout and campaign mobilization will favor the incumbent bloc, especially in decisive districts.
B) Turnout and mobilization will favor challengers or newly coordinated opposition forces in enough districts to block a supermajority.

Will one electoral bloc enter the 2026 election with a clear, sustained lead in national vote intention large enough to make a seat landslide plausible under Hungary’s electoral system?
A) Yes. One side—most likely Fidesz or a disciplined opposing bloc—will hold a sufficiently large and persistent vote-intention advantage that the electoral system could amplify it into two-thirds.
B) No. The national vote will be close enough, or fragmented enough, that no bloc is positioned for the kind of seat surge usually required for a supermajority.

Will the anti-Fidesz opposition be sufficiently unified in single-member districts to avoid major vote-splitting against Fidesz?
A) Yes. Opposition parties/candidates will coordinate effectively enough in most constituencies that anti-Fidesz votes are not heavily wasted.
B) No. Opposition forces will remain divided or only partially coordinated, causing enough district-level vote splitting to prevent a unified anti-Fidesz seat-maximizing strategy.

Has the geographic and institutional structure of Hungary’s electoral system remained strongly favorable to converting a modest Fidesz vote lead into a disproportionate seat bonus?
A) Yes. District geography, compensation rules, and the mixed system still strongly magnify Fidesz’s seat share relative to vote share.
B) No. The system’s pro-Fidesz amplification will be weaker than many assume, either because support has shifted geographically or because competitive districts are numerous enough to limit seat distortion.

Will there be meaningful legal, administrative, or electoral-rule changes before the 2026 election that materially affect the probability of a supermajority outcome?
A) Yes. Rule changes, candidacy rules, districting, media/administrative shifts, or other institutional interventions will materially shape the seat distribution and could push a bloc toward supermajority territory.
B) No. There will be no major rule or administrative changes with large electoral impact beyond the status quo already priced into expectations.

Will newly emergent or reorganized opposition forces maintain viability through election day rather than fragment, collapse, or lose coordination capacity?
A) Yes. A new or reconfigured opposition vehicle will remain organizationally coherent, electorally viable, and capable of national coordination through 2026.
B) No. New opposition formations will lose momentum, split internally, or fail to build durable local machinery, reducing their national competitiveness.

Will pre-election public opinion and local-election evidence by late 2025/early 2026 show Fidesz still dominant in a decisive share of competitive single-member districts?
A) Yes. District-level evidence will show Fidesz leading or highly competitive in enough constituencies that a large seat haul remains structurally likely.
B) No. District-level data will show many formerly safe or lean-Fidesz constituencies becoming genuinely competitive or opposition-leaning, reducing the chance of a supermajority.

Will economic and political conditions in Hungary by 2026 be favorable enough to the incumbent that broad anti-government tactical voting fails to consolidate?
A) Yes. Inflation, growth, scandals, EU-funds dynamics, and incumbent evaluation will be benign enough—or opposition weakness strong enough—that anti-government tactical voting does not fully cohere.
B) No. Economic strain, governance fatigue, scandals, or mobilized tactical voting will create a stronger anti-incumbent wave than incumbency advantages can offset.

Is there a realistic path for an opposition coalition, rather than Fidesz, to become the side that captures a seat bonus large enough to approach or exceed a supermajority?
A) Yes. An opposition coalition could, under plausible vote and coordination patterns, itself win a seat bonus large enough to threaten or obtain a supermajority.
B) No. Even if the opposition performs well, its likely best-case outcome is a simple majority or plurality, not a supermajority-scale seat conversion.

Will the opposition enter the 2026 election sufficiently unified in candidate coordination and/or list structure to avoid major anti-Fidesz vote-splitting in single-member districts?
A) No. The opposition will remain fragmented or only partially coordinated, allowing substantial vote-splitting in many districts.
B) Yes. The opposition will achieve effective coordination or unification, sharply reducing vote-splitting in districts.

Will Fidesz-KDNP retain enough national vote share by 2026 to remain clearly ahead of any rival bloc?
A) Yes. Fidesz-KDNP will retain a strong enough national lead to dominate both the list vote and many constituencies.
B) No. Fidesz-KDNP support will erode enough that it will no longer hold a clear nationwide advantage.

Will the electoral system’s seat-conversion effects be strong enough in 2026 that a modest Fidesz vote lead could still produce a two-thirds parliamentary supermajority?
A) Yes. Hungary’s mixed electoral rules and district dynamics will still amplify the winner enough that a moderate lead can yield a supermajority.
B) No. Even if Fidesz leads, vote-to-seat translation will not be strong enough in 2026 to push any bloc to a two-thirds majority.

Will there be any legally valid and electorally meaningful coalition arrangement after the election that should be counted as a single supermajority-winning bloc rather than separate parties short of the threshold?
A) Yes. A pre-election or post-election alliance/coalition will function as a coherent bloc and can realistically cross the supermajority threshold as a coalition.
B) No. No coalition arrangement likely to emerge will be both electorally meaningful and properly counted as a single supermajority-winning bloc.

Will the leading party or coalition enter the 2026 election facing a sufficiently fragmented opposition that it can win a disproportionate share of single-member districts?
A) The opposition will remain fragmented enough that the leading bloc can capture many districts with pluralities or modest majorities.
B) The opposition will be coordinated enough, or at least not fragmented enough, to deny the leading bloc the district sweep required for a supermajority.

Will Hungary’s electoral system in 2026 still convert a modest national vote lead for the leading bloc into a realistic path to a two-thirds seat share?
A) The electoral system and district structure will continue to strongly magnify the seat share of the largest bloc, leaving a credible route from ordinary victory to supermajority.
B) The electoral system may reward the largest bloc, but not enough under likely 2026 vote distributions to make a two-thirds seat share probable.

Is the dominant governing bloc likely to retain enough voter support by 2026 to finish clearly ahead of all rivals rather than merely competitive?
A) The dominant governing bloc will still command a sufficiently strong national vote base to finish clearly ahead and capitalize on the system’s seat bonus.
B) The dominant governing bloc will lose enough support that even if it wins, its margin will be too narrow to produce a supermajority.

Will opposition parties be willing and able to coordinate candidacies and tactical voting effectively enough to block a district-level landslide by the leading bloc?
A) Opposition coordination will be too weak, inconsistent, or late to prevent the leading bloc from sweeping enough single-member districts.
B) Opposition coordination and tactical voting will be effective enough in enough districts to block the seat concentration needed for a supermajority.

Will Fidesz or another leading bloc enter the 2026 election with a large enough national vote lead that the electoral system’s seat bonus can plausibly push it to two-thirds?
A) Yes. One bloc—most plausibly Fidesz—will likely hold a sufficiently clear national lead that district victories plus list compensation can compound into a two-thirds seat outcome.
B) No. The national vote gap will be too small—or the leader may even trail—so the electoral system alone is unlikely to generate a supermajority.

Will anti-Fidesz/opposition voters and parties coordinate efficiently enough at the district level to prevent severe vote-splitting in single-member constituencies?
A) Yes. Opposition/challenger coordination will be effective enough that anti-incumbent votes are not heavily fragmented in single-member districts.
B) No. Opposition/challenger forces will remain fragmented or poorly coordinated, allowing avoidable losses in many single-member districts.

Are incumbency advantages from media dominance, state resources, patronage networks, and rule-setting still strong enough in 2026 to materially inflate the leading incumbent bloc’s seat share beyond its raw vote share?
A) Yes. Incumbent structural advantages remain powerful and will materially increase seat conversion efficiency for the ruling bloc.
B) No. Structural incumbency advantages will be weaker, more contested, or insufficient to create the extra district wins needed for a supermajority.

Will the main challenger bloc be organizationally robust enough nationwide to convert polling support into constituency wins rather than underperforming on election day?
A) Yes. The main challenger has or will build the candidate quality, local organization, and turnout machinery needed to realize its polling strength across the country.
B) No. The challenger’s organization will be too thin, uneven, or inexperienced to translate support into constituency victories at scale.

Will the geographic distribution of support in 2026 be unusually efficient for one bloc, producing many narrow district wins rather than wasted surplus votes?
A) Yes. The leading bloc’s support will be distributed efficiently across districts, yielding many marginal wins and a large seat premium.
B) No. Support will be inefficiently distributed, with wasted majorities in strongholds and too few competitive district wins to reach two-thirds.

Could pre-election alliances or post-election coalition formation realistically unify enough seats under one governing banner to count as a supermajority coalition rather than merely a plurality government?
A) Yes. Coalition bargains are feasible enough that a bloc short of two-thirds on its own could still form a supermajority coalition.
B) No. Even if alliances emerge, ideological and strategic frictions make a true supermajority coalition unlikely.

Will the anti-Fidesz opposition coordinate effectively enough in single-member districts to avoid large vote-splitting losses?
A) Yes. Opposition coordination in constituencies is effective enough that anti-incumbent votes are not heavily split, making a supermajority much harder.
B) No. Opposition forces remain fragmented or coordinate poorly, splitting anti-Fidesz votes and allowing many district wins by the incumbent.

Will Fidesz retain vote support at or near the level needed for the electoral system to translate a plurality into a two-thirds seat majority?
A) No. Fidesz support slips below the practical level needed for a two-thirds seat outcome, even if it still wins overall.
B) Yes. Fidesz retains enough support that, under Hungary’s system, its vote share is sufficient for a plausible two-thirds seat majority.

Will the Hungarian electoral system’s seat bonus for the leading party remain large enough in practice that a modest national vote advantage can still produce a supermajority?
A) No. In the actual electoral environment, the seat bonus is insufficient to turn a normal lead into a supermajority without unusually strong vote margins.
B) Yes. The electoral system continues to generate a strong seat bonus, so even a moderate lead can produce a supermajority.

Will there be a major pre-election shock that substantially weakens the incumbent side relative to baseline expectations?
A) Yes. A scandal, economic downturn, protest wave, or EU-related crisis damages the incumbent enough to prevent a supermajority.
B) No. No major anti-incumbent shock materializes; expected vulnerabilities never become electorally decisive.

Will there be a major pre-election shock that substantially weakens the opposition or increases rally-around-incumbent dynamics?
A) No. No such pro-incumbent shock occurs; the race remains closer to baseline or moves against Fidesz.
B) Yes. A war-related, migration-related, security-related, or opposition-specific shock boosts incumbency or depresses the opposition.

Will smaller parties clear thresholds or otherwise convert opposition votes into seats efficiently rather than wasting them?
A) Yes. Opposition-aligned smaller parties and alliances convert votes into seats efficiently, minimizing wasted anti-Fidesz votes.
B) No. Opposition votes are inefficiently distributed or wasted via threshold failures, fragmentation, or poor alliance structure.

Will turnout and voter mobilization patterns disproportionately benefit Fidesz in a way that amplifies district-level seat wins?
A) No. Turnout patterns do not disproportionately favor Fidesz; urban/opposition mobilization is competitive or stronger.
B) Yes. Differential turnout and organizational strength favor Fidesz, especially in pivotal districts, magnifying seat gains.

Will the campaign and information environment remain sufficiently tilted toward the incumbent that opposition gains in public sentiment do not fully convert into votes/seats?
A) No. The information environment is not decisive enough to preserve a dominant incumbent advantage once support softens.
B) Yes. Media/control asymmetries and campaign-state overlap remain strong enough to suppress effective opposition conversion of sentiment into seats.

Will elite fragmentation inside Fidesz or its broader governing coalition remain negligible through the election?
A) Yes. Internal cohesion weakens enough—through defections, factionalism, or candidate-level conflict—to reduce the odds of a unified supermajority outcome.
B) No. Fidesz remains highly cohesive, avoiding internal splits that could jeopardize a supermajority.

Will legal, administrative, or electoral-rule changes before the election materially increase the incumbent’s ability to convert support into a supermajority?
A) No. There are no meaningful late rule changes or administrative shifts that improve the incumbent’s seat-conversion advantage.
B) Yes. Institutional or administrative changes before the election further improve the incumbent’s odds of translating support into a supermajority.
will-any-state-actor-use-chemical-weapon:
Will Russia's leadership judge that limited chemical weapons use in Ukraine would provide meaningful military or coercive benefit before May 1, 2026?
A) Russia's leadership will judge that limited chemical weapons use could provide meaningful military or coercive benefit in Ukraine.
B) Russia's leadership will not judge that limited chemical weapons use would provide enough military or coercive benefit to justify crossing the threshold.

Will expected international retaliation and escalation costs be strong enough to deter any state actor from using chemical weapons in Ukraine before May 1, 2026?
A) Expected international retaliation and escalation costs will not be strong enough to deter all state actors from chemical weapons use in Ukraine.
B) Expected international retaliation and escalation costs will be strong enough to deter all state actors from chemical weapons use in Ukraine.

Will battlefield or regime-pressure conditions in the war deteriorate enough to make chemical weapons use appear worth the risk to a state actor before May 1, 2026?
A) Battlefield or regime-pressure conditions will deteriorate enough that chemical weapons use will appear worth the risk to a state actor.
B) Battlefield or regime-pressure conditions will not deteriorate enough to make chemical weapons use appear worth the risk to any state actor.

Will there be an incident in Ukraine before May 1, 2026 that is both plausibly a chemical attack by a state actor and likely to be recognized as such under the question's intended standard?
A) There will be an incident in Ukraine before May 1, 2026 that is plausibly a chemical attack by a state actor and recognized as counting under the question.
B) No incident in Ukraine before May 1, 2026 will both plausibly involve state chemical weapons use and be recognized as counting under the question.

Do prior allegations of chemical or riot-control-agent use in the Russia-Ukraine war indicate a real escalation pathway toward clearer state chemical weapons use before May 1, 2026?
A) Prior allegations indicate a real escalation pathway toward clearer state chemical weapons use before May 1, 2026.
B) Prior allegations do not indicate a meaningful escalation pathway toward clearer state chemical weapons use before May 1, 2026.

Is a state actor in or around the Ukraine war likely to face battlefield or strategic incentives before May 1, 2026 that materially favor chemical-weapon use despite the political costs?
A) Yes. The military or coercive value of chemical use could become attractive under battlefield stress, stalemate, or escalation, making use a live option.
B) No. Conventional alternatives are sufficient, and CW would add little military value relative to the risks, so incentives stay weak.

Is international deterrence against chemical-weapon use in Ukraine strong enough to make deliberate state use very unlikely?
A) No. The expected diplomatic, military, and reputational costs dominate any plausible battlefield gains, so incentives remain negative.
B) Yes. Fear of severe retaliation, further isolation, and crossing a major taboo makes deliberate state use extremely unlikely.

Does the most relevant state actor already have the operational capability, command willingness, and delivery means to carry out a chemical attack in Ukraine on the forecast horizon?
A) Yes. The main candidate state actor has stocks/access, trained units or proxies, and practical delivery options, and senior leadership could authorize use.
B) No. Even if some capability exists in theory, operational readiness, chain-of-command willingness, or reliable delivery in this context is doubtful.

Is limited, localized, or deniable chemical-weapon use in Ukraine plausible on this timeline, rather than only large conspicuous attacks?
A) Yes. Small-scale or deniable use—against trenches, urban targets, or selected military positions—is a realistic pathway and more likely than a major attack.
B) No. Deniable or localized use is still too risky, too hard to control, or too easy to expose; if CW were used it would likely require a larger step leaders avoid.

Would a chemical incident in Ukraine, if it occurred, likely be attributable with enough confidence to a state actor for forecasters/resolvers to judge that the event happened?
A) Yes. If an incident occurs, intelligence, forensic evidence, or pattern-of-behavior evidence would probably permit a state-actor judgment.
B) No. Attribution would likely remain contested, with ambiguity, propaganda, and evidentiary gaps preventing a confident state-actor conclusion.

Is there a meaningful risk that escalation in the war before May 1, 2026 increases the probability of chemical use by a state actor?
A) Yes. Escalation dynamics—territorial losses, regime pressure, widened war, or perceived existential stakes—could raise the chance materially.
B) No. The conflict can remain intense without crossing this threshold; even worsening conditions need not make CW use substantially more likely.

Are norm-breaking patterns by the most relevant state actor strong evidence that chemical use in Ukraine is more plausible than base rates alone would suggest?
A) Yes. Prior poisonings, treaty violations allegations, and other norm-breaking behavior imply weaker restraint and higher conditional risk.
B) No. Past norm-breaking does not strongly transfer to battlefield CW use in Ukraine; this case has different stakes and constraints.

Is the relevant definition and adjudication standard likely broad enough that the sort of chemical use most plausibly attempted in Ukraine would count as 'chemical weapons use' for this question?
A) Yes. The likely mode of use would probably satisfy the question's standard and be recognized as chemical-weapons use rather than dismissed as ambiguity.
B) No. The most plausible incidents would fall into ambiguous categories, be disputed, or fail the resolution standard, so a true 'yes' remains unlikely even if something suspicious occurs.

Will the military and political leadership of the most plausible state actor judge that limited chemical weapon use in Ukraine would provide meaningful net battlefield or coercive utility before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. A plausible user—most likely Russia or Russian-controlled forces—could see localized chemical use as useful for flushing troops from trenches, degrading morale, shaping assaults, or imposing costs in ways conventional means do not.
B) No. Chemical weapons would add little beyond existing conventional fires and drones, while protective equipment, weather sensitivity, and operational complexity reduce their military value.

Will anticipated international costs of chemical weapon use in Ukraine remain credibly high enough to deter state authorization before May 1, 2026?
A) No. Decision-makers may believe international punishment will be limited, delayed, or manageable, especially for small-scale or ambiguous incidents that fall short of a mass-casualty attack.
B) Yes. Leaders still expect severe diplomatic, economic, legal, and possibly military consequences from confirmed CW use, making authorization unattractive.

Will the war in Ukraine enter a phase of acute escalation pressure or battlefield desperation that materially increases the appeal of chemical weapon use before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Severe battlefield setbacks, manpower strain, or fear of strategic defeat could push leaders toward riskier escalation options including chemical use.
B) No. Even if the war remains brutal, leaders can continue relying on conventional escalation tools rather than crossing the chemical threshold.

Will low-level or ambiguous uses of toxic chemicals by a state actor occur in a form that likely qualifies under the forecast's definition of chemical weapons before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Small-scale incidents involving choking, incapacitating, or riot-control-type agents in combat are plausible and may satisfy the question's criteria even without a large classic CW strike.
B) No. Alleged incidents will either remain below the threshold of the definition, involve non-qualifying agents, or fail to meet the evidentiary standard needed to count.

Will attribution of any qualifying chemical incident to a state actor in Ukraine be sufficiently clear and accepted for forecasters to count the event as a 'yes' before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Available intelligence, biomedical evidence, munitions analysis, and pattern of use would likely be enough for the forecasting community to judge that a state actor was responsible.
B) No. Fog of war, contested evidence, and propaganda will leave any suspected incident too disputed for many careful forecasters to score as a confirmed yes.

Will command-and-control over prohibited agents remain tight enough to prevent unauthorized, deniable, or locally initiated state-actor use before May 1, 2026?
A) No. Under battlefield stress, local commanders or security services may have enough access, incentive, or deniability to conduct limited use without airtight central restraint.
B) Yes. Central authorities understand the stakes and will keep strict control, making unauthorized or accidental qualifying use unlikely.

Will the chemical weapons norm continue to erode in this conflict through repeated small-scale incidents, making further state use more likely before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Repeated allegations, tolerated gray-zone use, and weak enforcement can lower psychological and political barriers, increasing the chance of additional qualifying incidents.
B) No. The norm remains resilient enough that even if there are allegations or isolated gray-area episodes, they do not meaningfully raise the odds of deliberate state CW employment.

Have Russian state forces already engaged in repeated chemical-weapons use in Ukraine, indicating an established pattern likely to continue or escalate?
A) Yes. Open-source reporting, Ukrainian claims, and Western government assessments indicate repeated use of riot-control or choking agents such as chloropicrin by Russian forces, so the barrier to future use is already broken.
B) No. The evidence to date is disputed, often concerns irritants or dual-use agents, and does not establish a robust pattern of CW use comparable to clear historical precedents.

Are the international military and political costs of chemical-weapons use in Ukraine low enough that a state actor could employ them without facing decisive new punishment?
A) Yes. Prior norm violations have produced condemnation and sanctions but not decisive battlefield consequences, suggesting deterrence is incomplete and limited CW use may be seen as tolerable.
B) No. Chemical use would risk major escalation in Western support, harsher sanctions, diplomatic isolation, and reputational damage, so deterrence remains meaningful.

Is battlefield pressure on Russian forces likely to become severe enough before May 1, 2026 to make chemical use tactically attractive?
A) Yes. Attritional warfare, manpower constraints, and the need to clear trenches or fortified positions could intensify incentives for localized chemical employment.
B) No. Russia can continue prosecuting the war with conventional means, drones, glide bombs, and artillery, reducing any need to incur the risks of chemical escalation.

Can a state actor employ chemical agents in Ukraine in a deniable, limited, or legally ambiguous way that still counts as chemical-weapons use?
A) Yes. Agents such as chloropicrin or riot-control compounds can be delivered in small munitions and framed as nonlethal, dual-use, or hard-to-verify incidents, making use operationally feasible while preserving some deniability.
B) No. Truly countable chemical-weapons use is hard to hide; deployment, symptoms, samples, and intelligence collection raise the odds of exposure, so deniability is weaker than the high-probability view assumes.

Is command-and-control over Russian or Russian-aligned forces tight enough to prevent unauthorized or locally initiated chemical use?
A) No. Frontline conditions, decentralized operations, and variable discipline make local or semi-authorized chemical use plausible even without explicit top-level orders.
B) Yes. The Russian state has strong incentives to control escalation and can largely prevent unauthorized use of proscribed agents by regular or proxy forces.

Would any chemical use in Ukraine be detected and attributed with sufficient confidence to count for this forecast, rather than remain too ambiguous or contested?
A) Yes. At least some incidents would likely produce enough forensic, intelligence, or official confirmation to be recognized as state-actor chemical use for the purpose of resolution.
B) No. Many alleged incidents would remain evidentially murky, unattributed, or excluded by stricter definitions, so even if something borderline occurred it may not resolve as a clear 'yes'.

Before May 1, 2026, will Russia's leadership perceive a significant military or coercive advantage from limited chemical weapons use in Ukraine that conventional options cannot achieve as effectively?
A) Yes. Limited chemical use could be seen as offering tactical advantages in trench clearing, area denial, psychological shock, or coercive signaling beyond what conventional means are achieving.
B) No. Russian leadership would judge that conventional weapons, drones, missiles, and manpower tools already provide enough options, leaving chemical use with little added military value.

If a Russian state unit used a chemical agent in Ukraine before May 1, 2026, would the Kremlin expect attribution and international retaliation to be limited enough to make such use tolerable?
A) Yes. The Kremlin would expect that attribution could remain contested or consequences would be mostly rhetorical, making limited use an acceptable risk.
B) No. The Kremlin would expect high confidence attribution and severe diplomatic, economic, or military consequences, making use too costly.

Before May 1, 2026, will battlefield or political pressures on Russia in Ukraine deteriorate enough to make escalation to chemical use appear worth the risk?
A) Yes. Russian setbacks, attrition, domestic pressure, or perceived need to break stalemate could intensify enough to make chemical escalation attractive.
B) No. Even under pressure, Russia would still prefer other escalation tools over crossing the chemical threshold.

Is low-scale, deniable chemical-agent use by Russian forces in Ukraine operationally feasible and politically controllable before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Russia can conduct small-scale or covert use in ways that are hard to verify, easier to deny, and unlikely to spiral uncontrollably.
B) No. Chemical use would be too hard to contain, too likely to be detected, or too operationally unreliable to be an attractive deniable option.

Before May 1, 2026, will any other state actor besides Russia have a non-negligible chance of chemical weapons use in Ukraine?
A) Yes. Another state actor's involvement is unlikely but still materially possible, so the event space is broader than Russia alone.
B) No. Realistically only Russia matters; other state actors have near-zero likelihood, so they do not materially raise the probability.

Is a major battlefield or strategic deterioration for Russian forces in Ukraine likely before May 1, 2026?
A) Russian forces are likely to face severe setbacks or threats to strategically important positions, increasing pressure to consider extreme escalation options.
B) Russian forces are unlikely to face enough battlefield deterioration to seriously consider chemical escalation.

Would the Russian leadership view chemical weapons use as providing meaningful military utility in the Ukraine theater?
A) Chemical agents could meaningfully degrade Ukrainian personnel, fortifications, or logistics in ways conventional munitions cannot easily achieve.
B) Chemical weapons would offer little additional battlefield value compared with available conventional fires and would create operational complications.

Would anticipated international retaliation meaningfully deter a state actor from using chemical weapons in Ukraine?
A) Expected retaliation would be limited, slow, or uncertain enough that it would not decisively deter use.
B) Expected retaliation would be severe and credible enough to strongly deter any state actor from use.

Is reliable attribution of chemical weapons use in Ukraine likely enough to make covert or plausibly deniable use unattractive?
A) A state actor could plausibly employ chemicals in a way that creates enough ambiguity to avoid confident attribution or delay consensus.
B) Attribution capabilities are strong enough that any meaningful use would likely be identified and pinned on the perpetrating state actor.

Is the relevant definition of 'chemical weapons use' likely to include ambiguous agents or delivery methods that a state actor might consider below the threshold of major escalation?
A) Ambiguous cases such as incapacitating agents, riot-control agents in combat, or toxic industrial chemicals used deliberately are realistic pathways that could count as chemical weapons use.
B) Only clear use of internationally recognized warfare agents is likely, making threshold-crossing use less likely than ambiguous low-level incidents.

Have state actors in the Ukraine war already used prohibited chemical warfare agents, rather than merely being accused of doing so?
A) Yes. There have already been real uses of prohibited chemical warfare agents by state actors in the conflict, even if publicly contested.
B) No. Public allegations do not amount to established prior use of prohibited chemical warfare agents by state actors.

Have alleged toxic-agent incidents in Ukraine been independently verified at a level strong enough to indicate an ongoing pattern of state chemical weapons use?
A) Yes. The available reporting, samples, medical signatures, or intelligence are strong enough to treat these incidents as a genuine pattern rather than noise or propaganda.
B) No. Existing allegations are too weak, too ambiguous, too politicized, or too poorly substantiated to infer a real pattern.

Would a state actor in this war gain meaningful battlefield or coercive advantage from using chemical weapons before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Chemical weapons could provide tactical benefits in trenches, enclosed positions, urban clearing, or psychological disruption that conventional means do not fully replicate.
B) No. Any military benefit would be marginal, unreliable, or duplicative of conventional fires, making use irrational.

Would the expected diplomatic, military, and legal costs of chemical weapons use in Ukraine be severe enough to deter a state actor from doing it?
A) No. The likely costs are limited, manageable, or already priced in, so deterrence is weak.
B) Yes. The political and strategic costs would be substantial enough to deter state actors from crossing this line.

Is attribution of chemical-agent use in Ukraine likely to remain sufficiently ambiguous that a state actor could use such weapons and plausibly avoid decisive punishment?
A) Yes. Ambiguity is high enough that limited use could occur without universally accepted attribution or overwhelming retaliation.
B) No. Attribution capabilities are good enough that state use would likely be exposed and punished.

Are riot-control agents or other toxic chemicals likely to be used in ways that would meet the resolution criteria for 'chemical weapons use' by a state actor?
A) Yes. State actors are likely to use toxic chemicals in ways that cross the operative threshold for the question.
B) No. Likely toxic-agent incidents would either not occur or would fall outside the resolution’s intended threshold.

Is the conflict likely to remain intense enough before May 1, 2026 to create circumstances where chemical escalation becomes tempting?
A) Yes. The war will remain active and contested enough that incentives for unconventional escalation persist through the deadline.
B) No. The conflict will de-intensify, freeze, or otherwise reduce incentives for this form of escalation before the deadline.

Do state actors with forces operating in or over Ukraine possess accessible stocks, delivery systems, and command willingness to employ chemical agents on the relevant timeline?
A) Yes. Relevant state actors have the means and practical readiness to employ such agents if they choose.
B) No. Even if stockpiles exist, practical deployment constraints or command reluctance make actual use unlikely.

Will battlefield or political pressures on the main relevant state actor(s), especially Russia, become severe enough before May 1, 2026 that leaders seriously consider chemical weapons use as a useful escalation option in Ukraine?
A) Yes. Battlefield setbacks, manpower strain, domestic political stakes, or a need to break stalemate could create strong incentives to consider chemical use.
B) No. Even under pressure, leaders will still view chemical use as too risky, unnecessary, or operationally marginal to seriously pursue.

Would the expected international and military costs of state chemical weapons use in Ukraine be high enough to deter authorization?
A) Yes. The diplomatic, economic, legal, and possibly military consequences would be severe enough that leaders avoid crossing this line.
B) No. Consequences would be limited, manageable, or already mostly priced in, so deterrence is weak.

Does the relevant state actor retain a practical capability to deploy chemical agents in Ukraine in a way that could achieve tactical or coercive effects?
A) Yes. The actor has stockpiles, delivery means, trained units, or dual-use industrial capacity sufficient for real operational use.
B) No. Effective battlefield deployment capability is degraded, too cumbersome, too risky, or not available in usable form.

Would chemical weapons likely provide meaningful military or coercive utility in the Ukraine theater relative to available conventional alternatives?
A) Yes. Chemical agents could help clear trenches, enclosed spaces, or fortified positions, terrorize civilians, or signal willingness to escalate.
B) No. Chemical weapons would add little militarily beyond conventional fires, while complicating operations and risking blowback.

If a state actor used chemical weapons in Ukraine, is it likely that the use would be detectably attributable in a way that raises the expected cost to the perpetrator?
A) Yes. Modern surveillance, intelligence collection, environmental sampling, and public scrutiny make successful concealment unlikely.
B) No. Use could be ambiguous, deniable, or too hard to prove conclusively, reducing the expected penalty for the perpetrator.

Will Russian or other state decision-makers judge limited chemical weapons use in Ukraine to provide meaningful battlefield or coercive advantages before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Limited use is likely to be seen as operationally useful for clearing positions, degrading defenders, or creating localized panic, especially in an attritional war.
B) No. Chemical weapons are likely to be seen as offering little durable advantage relative to conventional fires, drones, and thermobarics, especially given operational complications.

Will expected external costs of chemical weapons use in Ukraine before May 1, 2026 be severe enough to deter a state actor that is otherwise militarily pressured?
A) No. The marginal diplomatic, military, and economic penalties are likely to be viewed as limited, delayed, or largely already priced in, reducing deterrent effect.
B) Yes. The risk of sharper sanctions, loss of remaining partners, intelligence exposure, and possible escalation would be judged substantial enough to deter use.

Do existing allegations, intelligence signals, and past poison or chemical incidents indicate an active state capacity-and-intent trajectory toward battlefield chemical use in Ukraine rather than isolated, ambiguous, or non-comparable events?
A) Yes. The pattern of prior poisonings, norm violations, and repeated allegations points to both willingness and practical preparation for chemical use under deniable conditions.
B) No. The evidence is too ambiguous or non-comparable to show a genuine trajectory toward battlefield chemical use in Ukraine; past incidents do not strongly predict this outcome.

Is it likely that at least one incident meeting a reasonable standard for 'state actor use of chemical weapons in Ukraine' will both occur and be credibly attributable before May 1, 2026?
