A) If chemical weapons are used, detection and attribution are likely to be good enough that the event will be recognized as state-actor use.
B) Any possible incident would likely remain ambiguous, deniable, or below the threshold needed to confidently classify it as state-actor chemical weapons use.

Have state actors already used prohibited chemical agents in Ukraine during the current war?
A) Yes. There is already credible evidence that state actors have used prohibited chemical agents in Ukraine, implying the threshold has already been crossed in practice.
B) No. There has not yet been sufficiently credible, verified state use of prohibited chemical agents in Ukraine; allegations remain ambiguous, limited, or unproven.

Would limited battlefield use of riot control agents or other toxic chemicals in Ukraine qualify under the question’s intended meaning of 'chemical weapons'?
A) Yes. The intended resolution should include use of riot control agents or other toxic chemicals as methods of warfare if employed by a state actor in Ukraine.
B) No. The question should be read more narrowly, excluding marginal/toxic irritant cases and focusing on classic chemical warfare agents or clearly prohibited battlefield use.

Do one or more state actors fighting in or around Ukraine currently retain operational stockpiles, delivery means, and trained units capable of employing chemical agents on short notice?
A) Yes. At least one relevant state actor has usable agents, delivery systems, and doctrine sufficient for near-term employment.
B) No. Relevant state actors either lack practical readiness for CW use in this theater or would face too many operational constraints to employ them effectively.

Would a state actor expect severe and credible military, economic, or political retaliation if it used chemical weapons in Ukraine before May 1, 2026?
A) No. Expected retaliation is limited, uncertain, or tolerable, so deterrence is weak.
B) Yes. Retaliation risk is substantial and credible, creating strong deterrence against use.

Have chemical agents demonstrated enough battlefield utility in the Ukraine war environment to make future state use materially attractive?
A) Yes. Chemical agents can clear positions, degrade defenders, create fear, and complement trench/static warfare enough to be useful.
B) No. Chemical agents offer little incremental advantage under current battlefield conditions relative to conventional alternatives.

Is attribution likely to be sufficiently reliable, in real time or after the fact, that a state actor would expect its chemical use in Ukraine to be detected and pinned on it?
A) No. Fog of war, access constraints, and evidentiary ambiguity make attribution difficult, reducing expected costs to the user.
B) Yes. Intelligence collection and forensic processes are good enough that state actors would expect attribution and punishment.

Are frontline dynamics and escalation pressures in Ukraine likely to worsen enough before May 1, 2026 to make chemical use more tempting as a coercive or tactical option?
A) Yes. Battlefield stress, stalemate, manpower strain, or fear of defeat are likely to intensify enough to increase incentive for escalation.
B) No. The conflict is likely to remain within its current escalation band, without pressures strong enough to make CW use attractive.

Is there credible evidence that command authorities of relevant state actors are willing to authorize norm-breaking WMD-adjacent actions when under pressure in this conflict?
A) Yes. Relevant leadership has shown willingness to authorize actions that violate strong international norms when they perceive military necessity or impunity.
B) No. Relevant command authorities remain constrained by strategic caution, internal controls, and concern over crossing a major taboo.

Would any future chemical incident in Ukraine more likely come from a state actor than from non-state actors, industrial release, sabotage, or false/misattributed reporting?
A) Yes. If a chemical event occurs in Ukraine, the most likely culprit is a state actor rather than an accidental or non-state source.
B) No. Many reported or future incidents could stem from industrial chemicals, accidental releases, non-state use, or misinterpretation rather than state action.

Is any state actor fighting in or operating in Ukraine likely to perceive a meaningful military or coercive advantage from chemical-weapons use before May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Chemical use could be seen as offering tactical advantages in trench/fortification clearing, psychological disruption, or localized area denial that conventional means do not reliably provide.
B) No. Chemical use would add little militarily compared with available conventional fires, drones, thermobarics, and siege tactics, so there is little practical advantage.

Will decision-makers of a relevant state actor judge the expected political, military, and escalation costs of chemical-weapons use in Ukraine to be tolerable?
A) Yes. The actor would expect that international punishment, retaliation, or escalation would be limited, delayed, or manageable relative to the perceived benefits.
B) No. The actor would judge the diplomatic, military, and reputational costs—including possible escalation and stronger foreign support to Ukraine—as too high to justify use.

Is a relevant state actor both willing and able to deploy a qualifying chemical agent in Ukraine under conditions where the event would likely be recognized as state use?
A) Yes. The actor has access to suitable agents/delivery methods and enough confidence in deniability, compartmentation, or operational control to carry out a qualifying attack.
B) No. Even if some capability exists, operational, command, and attribution risks make actual qualifying use unlikely; any attempts would more likely be avoided, fail, or stay below the threshold of recognized state use.

Are battlefield or strategic conditions in Ukraine likely to deteriorate enough before May 1, 2026 to increase incentives for unusually escalatory weapons employment?
A) Yes. Military setbacks, manpower strain, attritional stalemate, or pressure to break defenses are likely to intensify enough to make chemical escalation more attractive.
B) No. The conflict is likely to remain within current patterns or de-escalate enough that incentives for chemical escalation do not materially increase.

If a suspicious toxic-agent incident occurs, is it likely to meet the resolution standard for 'state actor use of chemical weapons in Ukraine' rather than remain ambiguous, disputed, or excluded as non-qualifying?
A) Yes. Any real incident is likely to produce enough evidence, attribution, and definitional clarity that forecasters/resolvers would classify it as state chemical-weapons use in Ukraine.
B) No. Most alleged incidents would remain contested, insufficiently evidenced, or fall outside the resolution criteria, so they would not resolve as state actor chemical-weapons use.

Have prior alleged chemical-agent incidents in Ukraine reflected a genuine pattern of state willingness to employ prohibited or quasi-prohibited agents, rather than isolated, ambiguous, or misclassified events?
A) Repeated allegations and reporting are best explained by a real pattern of growing willingness to use chemical or chemical-adjacent agents in theater.
B) Prior allegations are too ambiguous, weakly verified, or better explained by confusion around smoke, munitions effects, or isolated misuse to establish a meaningful pattern of state chemical use.

Would the military or tactical benefits of chemical use in Ukraine be substantial enough in plausible 2025-2026 battlefield conditions to outweigh expected political, diplomatic, and escalation costs?
A) Plausible battlefield scenarios exist in which chemical use would offer meaningful tactical advantages, especially in trench, bunker, or urban positions, making use attractive under pressure.
B) Chemical use would provide little durable military advantage relative to conventional alternatives, while creating outsized strategic and diplomatic downside.

Is international deterrence against chemical weapons use by a state actor in Ukraine still strong enough to prevent even limited or deniable use before May 1, 2026?
A) Deterrence has eroded enough that a state actor may judge the marginal costs of limited or deniable use to be manageable.
B) Deterrence remains strong because any confirmed state chemical use would trigger severe political costs, possible military consequences, and loss of third-party support.

Is the most likely path to a qualifying event a localized, deniable, small-scale use of choking, incapacitating, or riot-control-type agents rather than a large, unmistakable mass-casualty attack?
A) A qualifying event is more likely to be a small-scale, deniable, front-line use than a dramatic strategic attack, which makes occurrence materially more likely.
B) If chemical weapons are used, they would likely need to be unmistakable to matter militarily, but that kind of use is exactly what remains least likely because it is hardest to hide and most costly.

Are command-and-control structures and state oversight in the relevant forces tight enough that unauthorized or semi-authorized chemical use is unlikely to occur and still count as state action?
A) Command environments are permissive enough that limited chemical use could be approved implicitly or explicitly at some level and still constitute state action.
B) Command-and-control is sufficiently centralized, and state leaders sufficiently aware of the taboo, that unauthorized or gray-zone chemical use is unlikely to occur as attributable state action.

If battlefield conditions deteriorate for Russia, does that meaningfully increase the probability that Russian leadership would authorize chemical weapons use in Ukraine for coercive, terror, or tactical purposes?
A) Yes. Severe battlefield setbacks, manpower strain, or threats to strategic objectives would increase incentives for escalation and coercive innovation, making CW authorization materially more likely.
B) No. Even under setbacks, Russian leadership would still view CW use as offering limited battlefield gain relative to enormous escalation, legitimacy, and command risks.

Would limited, deniable, or legally gray forms of toxic-agent use (for example incapacitating agents, riot-control agents in combat, or exploitation of toxic industrial chemicals) be treated by decision-makers as crossing a substantially lower threshold than classic nerve/blister agent attacks?
A) Yes. Decision-makers may perceive small-scale, deniable, or dual-use toxic employment as militarily useful and politically more survivable than overt large-scale CW attacks, lowering the effective barrier to use.
B) No. Even limited or ambiguous toxic-agent use would still be recognized as chemical warfare or dangerously close to it, so the taboo and deterrent costs remain high.

Are the expected international and military costs of Russian state chemical weapons use in Ukraine credibly high enough to deter such use through May 1, 2026?
A) No. International punishment is likely to be limited, delayed, or mostly symbolic relative to Russia's wartime stakes, so deterrence by external costs is weaker than often assumed.
B) Yes. The prospect of severe diplomatic, economic, military, and possibly escalatory consequences remains a strong deterrent, especially for a state already under scrutiny.

Does Russia currently retain the operational capability, logistical readiness, and command willingness to employ chemical weapons in Ukraine without prohibitive internal friction or exposure risk?
A) Yes. Russia likely has sufficient residual stocks, expertise, delivery means, and organizational capacity to conduct at least limited CW use if leadership chooses.
B) No. Operational readiness is doubtful: stocks may be degraded, delivery and handling are risky, command channels are cautious, and exposure/attribution risks impede real use.

Is prior Russian behavior involving chemical agents or tolerance of chemical use in other theaters predictive of future state chemical weapon use in Ukraine?
A) Yes. Prior conduct signals lower normative restraint, greater institutional familiarity with chemical agents, and a demonstrated willingness to absorb reputational costs.
B) No. Cross-theater or prior isolated incidents do not reliably predict wartime battlefield use in Ukraine, where the strategic context and scrutiny are different.

Does the risk of poor attribution, ambiguity, or information warfare meaningfully enable actual state chemical weapons use by reducing expected punishment?
A) Yes. If attribution is contested or delayed, expected costs fall and leaders may judge limited CW use as feasible under the fog of war.
B) No. Attribution capacity is good enough, and leaders would expect eventual exposure; ambiguity would not meaningfully shield a state actor from retaliation or stigma.

Will any state actor fighting in or directly operating in Ukraine judge that chemical weapons use would provide meaningful military or coercive advantage relative to available conventional alternatives?
A) No. Chemical weapons would offer little incremental advantage over artillery, drones, thermobarics, and other tools already available, especially in dispersed modern combat.
B) Yes. In some scenarios, chemical agents are seen as useful for flushing troops from positions, terrorizing civilians, degrading morale, or compensating for manpower or ammunition constraints.

Will the expected political, diplomatic, and military costs of chemical weapons use remain credibly high enough to deter state actors through May 1, 2026?
A) Yes. Decision-makers continue to expect severe reputational, sanctions, military-support, and escalation consequences from any confirmed chemical use.
B) No. Decision-makers come to believe the international response would be limited, delayed, or largely symbolic, reducing deterrence.

Is there a realistic pathway by which battlefield stress, territorial reversals, or leadership desperation could lead to deliberate escalation to chemical use?
A) No. Even under pressure, leaders do not see chemical use as a workable escape valve; desperation does not cross the threshold into this form of escalation.
B) Yes. Severe setbacks, regime-security fears, or acute battlefield crises create a genuine escalation pathway to deliberate chemical use.

Will command-and-control over relevant toxic agents, delivery systems, and authorization processes remain tight enough to prevent unauthorized or semi-authorized use?
A) Yes. Stocks, agents, and delivery mechanisms remain under centralized control, making accidental, freelance, or loosely authorized use unlikely.
B) No. Fragmented control, delegation, or local initiative creates room for unauthorized, deniable, or tacitly tolerated use.

Will ambiguous precursor events—such as use of riot-control agents, toxic industrial chemicals, sabotage of hazardous facilities, or prior poisoning behavior—prove to be genuine indicators of escalation risk rather than mostly noise?
A) No. These incidents are mostly ambiguous or non-predictive; they do not meaningfully signal imminent state CW use.
B) Yes. Seemingly marginal incidents are early signals of willingness to experiment, normalize, or probe the response to chemical-adjacent methods.

Will attribution after a suspected chemical incident in Ukraine be sufficiently fast and credible to shape state decision-making in advance?
A) Yes. States expect that a meaningful attack would likely be detected and attributed with enough confidence to trigger punishment, limiting the value of deniability.
B) No. Attribution is expected to be contested, delayed, or politically muddied, making deniable use more attractive.

Are the actors with both capability and access to Ukraine more willing than generally assumed to violate the chemical weapons taboo if they believe enforcement will be weak or deniable?
A) No. Relevant state actors remain more constrained by norms, treaty obligations, and fear of consequences than alarmists expect.
B) Yes. At least one relevant state actor is more willing than widely assumed to breach the taboo if it sees operational benefit and manageable consequences.

Will the conflict’s trajectory by 2025–2026 increase rather than reduce incentives for norm-breaking escalation?
A) No. Either the war de-intensifies, stabilizes, or adapts in ways that lower incentives for major taboo-breaking escalation.
B) Yes. The war evolves in ways—stalemate, attrition, looming defeat, cross-border widening, or political instability—that heighten incentives for norm-breaking escalation.

Will the strongest candidate’s overseas performance—especially in China and other key international markets—be sufficient to compensate for softer domestic grosses if needed?

Will franchise fatigue and audience fragmentation remain limited enough that at least one sequel/brand-driven film can still break through to exceptional global box office?

Is the pre-May-2026 release slate likely to contain at least one genuinely top-tier billion-dollar-caliber title that actually opens on schedule?

Has the global theatrical market for event films recovered enough that a strong tentpole can still realistically reach $1 billion worldwide under current conditions?

Will international markets provide enough box office support for a Hollywood or global release to bridge the gap from a good run to $1 billion?
